title: Multi-Granularity Hybrid-MAE-JSCC for Haptic-Assisted Semantic Image Transmission in Immersive XR
authors: Yucheng Liu; Chaowei Wang; Fan Jiang; Wenyuan Wang
abstract: Mobile XR applications require reliable transmission of visually detailed and materially consistent content over bandwidth-constrained, time-varying wireless channels. Existing Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC) methods, however, often struggle to preserve both global semantics at low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and fine texture at high SNRs. We propose a visual–haptic Hybrid-MAE-JSCC framework that represents the source at complementary global, local, and material-semantic granularities. An asymmetric Masked Autoencoder (MAE) branch models global context from visible patches, a lightweight ResNet branch preserves high-frequency texture, and a haptic encoder extracts material-aware tokens from synchronized vibration signals. At the receiver, gated cross-modal fusion injects these tactile cues into the visual latent representation while supporting haptic recovery and material classification. Experiments over AWGN and Rayleigh fading channels show improvements in pixel fidelity, perceptual quality, haptic reconstruction, and material-semantic consistency relative to the considered baselines and ablations.

title: Dose-dependent cardiac autonomic dysregulation under classroom crowding: heart rate variability analysis and machine learning classification
authors: Mohamed Naeem
abstract: Abstract Classroom overcrowding affects hundreds of millions of students globally, yet its physiological impact on cardiac autonomic function remains uncharacterized. This controlled within-subjects experiment enrolled 30 healthy university students who attended standardized 30-min lectures under three calibrated density conditions: low (30 students/150 m 2 ), medium (60/150 m 2 ), and high (100/150 m 2 ), with all environmental parameters held constant. Twenty-five heart rate variability (HRV) parameters spanning time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear domains were extracted from continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings. Subjective workload was assessed via the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and RoBoSS-SVM (a Support Vector Machine using the Robust, Bounded, Sparse, and Smooth loss function) with Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) classified density conditions from HRV features. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant density effects on all 25 HRV parameters (all p < 0.001), with 64% demonstrating exceptionally large effect sizes ( η 2 p ≥ 0.50). Parasympathetic markers showed the largest responses: pNN50 declined 52% ( η 2 p = 0.702), HF power declined 51% ( η 2 p = 0.654), and RMSSD declined 32% ( η 2 p = 0.420) from low to high density—while sympathetically influenced indices showed substantially smaller effects, confirming parasympathetic withdrawal as the predominant autonomic mechanism. These suppression magnitudes approach levels associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. NASA-TLX scores increased 74% across conditions ( p < 0.001) and correlated with HRV vagal indices ( r = −0.69 to −0.76), providing corroborating, though not definitive, evidence that crowding engages both subjective and autonomic stress pathways (see Discussion for caveats regarding this association). Temporal analysis confirmed progressive autonomic suppression without habituation across 10-min windows. RoBoSS-SVM achieved 92.2% accuracy for three-class discrimination and 97.2% accuracy (AUC = 0.993) for binary classification, with parasympathetic time-domain features comprising 64% of the optimal feature set. Classroom spatial density produces dose-dependent, mechanism-specific cardiac autonomic dysregulation dominated by vagal withdrawal—consistent with polyvagal theory’s prediction for social-environmental stressors. The excellent classification performance supports feasibility of real-time wearable monitoring for evidence-based classroom capacity management.

title: Current perspectives on smart grid cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection
authors: Nilesh Jain
abstract: The increasing convergence of renewable energy sources, information and communication technology, Internet of Things devices, smart meters, and phasor measurement units has enhanced the efficiency, reliability, and real-time operation of Smart Grids. However, this interconnected cyber-physical infrastructure has also increased cybersecurity vulnerabilities and attack surfaces. This paper reviews AI/ML-based security approaches for Smart Grid cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, focusing on major threats such as False Data Injection Attacks, Denial-of-Service attacks, Man-in-the-Middle attacks, spoofing, malware, and malicious command injection. The study examines existing protection mechanisms, including authentication and access control, intrusion detection, attack mitigation, secure communication, data protection, and privacy preservation. The study further discusses cyber-physical system protection, resilience, incident response, continuous monitoring, network segmentation, and AI/ML-based security approaches. A review of recent research highlights advances in anomaly detection, trust management, multilayer security, and intelligent threat detection. However, challenges remain in scalability, real-time processing, interoperability, adaptive defense, limited datasets, and real-world validation. The findings emphasize the need for integrated, intelligent, scalable, and adaptive cybersecurity approaches to strengthen Smart Grid resilience, reliability, availability, and operational continuity.

title: Plea for a theory of open texture
authors: Allison Koslow
abstract: Abstract I will consider a class of cases sometimes said to exemplify the open texture of language. They resemble some cases familiar from the mid-20th century. Consider J. L. Austin’s famous example of a bird that, for all the world, looks like a goldfinch, and then blows up like a grenade. Is it a goldfinch? A more realistic case involves the word “book” as used around 2000: were utterances such as eBooks are books true around this time? Hard to say. We can imagine a separation, where British speakers affirmed such sentences, and Americans denied them, without either appearing to misapply “book.” Is this kind of open texture a more well-studied linguistic phenomenon? I argue, first, that such cases resist both metaphysical and epistemic explanations. Then I argue that openness cannot be identified with partial definition, vagueness, non-vagueness indeterminacy, or underdetermination. This provides reason to think that, if there is any such thing as open texture, it is sui generis and worthy of its own theory.

title: TD-interpreter: enhancing the understanding of timing diagrams with visual-language learning
authors: Jie He; Vincent Theo Willem Kenbeek; Zhantao Yang; Meixun Qu; Ezio Bartocci; Dejan Ničković; Radu Grosu
abstract: Abstract We introduce TD-Interpreter, a specialised machine learning (ML) workflow that assists engineers in understanding complex timing diagrams (TDs), originating from a third party, during their design and verification process. The outcome of this workflow is a visual question-answer environment which allows engineers to input a set of TDs and ask design and verification queries regarding these TDs. To address limited training data availability, we developed a synthetic data generation pipeline that aligns visual information with its textual interpretation. We then implemented TD-Interpreter using a lightweight 7B Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), guided by both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). We also developed extensive TD-reasoning benchmarks from simple retrieval tasks to complex reasoning problems in the real world. Our experimental results show that TD-Interpreter substantially outperformed both the untuned base model, and commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.2), on the evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed workflow.

title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
authors: Minxian Xu; Jingfeng Wu; Shengye Song; Satish Narayana Srirama; Bahman Javad; Rajiv Ranjan; Devki Nandan Jha; Sa Wang; Wenhong Tian; Huanle Xu; Li Li; Zizhao Mo; Shuo Ren; Thomas Kunz; Petar Kochovski; Vlado Stankovski; Kejiang Ye; Chengzhong Xu; Rajkumar Buyya
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. Results Our analysis reveals that supporting LLMs at scale requires a transition from general‐purpose cloud infrastructure toward LLM‐aware, cross‐layer, and adaptive systems. Existing approaches have improved distributed execution, elastic resource management, multi‐tenant serving, and hardware utilization, but important gaps remain in cross‐layer coordination, workload‐aware orchestration, data and context management, interoperability, security, and system‐level optimization. Based on these gaps, we develop a research agenda covering future directions in sparse and heterogeneous computation, LLM‐enhanced system software, prompt and context management, autonomous cloud management, decentralized intelligence, edge‐cloud collaboration, personalized LLM services, and emerging computing paradigms. Conclusion Cloud‐native and distributed systems will play a central role in enabling the next generation of LLM services. Future infrastructures should evolve toward more intelligent, elastic, interoperable, secure, and heterogeneous platforms that jointly optimize computation, memory, communication, data, and service objectives. Continued advances in system design, standardization, and cross‐disciplinary collaboration will be essential for realizing scalable and sustainable LLM infrastructures.

title: Not an A11y: How Android Accessibility Exposes Mobile AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
authors: Rahul Deivasigamani; Sayeda Faatin Alvi; Derqui Andrea; Kaushal Punjabi; Stjepan Picek
abstract: The rise of autonomous AI agents represents a major paradigm shift in how users interact with mobile devices. Frameworks such as MobileRun and Mobile-Use can autonomously navigate Android applications and execute complex multi-step tasks. To interpret user interfaces, these frameworks rely primarily on Android accessibility (A11y) trees and secondarily on visual screenshots. In this paper, we demonstrate that this architectural dependence on unsanitized accessibility metadata, together with visual input, introduces a systemic vulnerability to indirect prompt injection. We show that adversarial prompts can cause autonomous agents to abandon their original objectives, violate context boundaries, and perform unauthorized device actions. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates goal hijacking, context drift, and unauthorized actions across visually hidden and fully exposed attack scenarios. In aggregate, MobileRun reaches an attack success rate of 0.822 with Gemma4:31B, while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B reduces this to 0.150 but does not eliminate context drift or unauthorized actions. These findings reveal that current mobile agent frameworks fail to enforce semantic context boundaries, treating passive environmental text as trusted instructions. Finally, we present a taxonomy of these attacks and discuss the need for zero-trust input validation, dedicated security agents, and strict context isolation within mobile agent architectures.

title: SemPurify: Semantics-Aware Data Purification for Black-box Backdoor Defense
authors: Jiawei Yu; Syed Irfan Ali Meerza; Yi Wu; Amir Sadovnik; Jian Liu
abstract: Backdoor attacks have emerged as a critical security threat in machine learning, where adversaries embed triggers within poisoned training samples to manipulate a model's predictions on targeted inputs while leaving its general behavior unaffected. This stealthy nature makes backdoor attacks difficult to detect, as the model functions normally until activated by a specific malicious trigger. Current purification-based defenses use image transformations (e.g., blurring) to disrupt trigger patterns but often degrade image quality. Even with advanced restoration techniques like diffusion models, these approaches can still alter visual or semantic information, reducing utility for downstream tasks. To address this, we propose the first semantics-aware data purification framework for black-box backdoor defense, SemPurify, which explicitly incorporates multi-level semantics (i.e., low-level semantic embeddings and high-level image tags) within a text-to-image (T2I) framework to guide image restoration during purification. Using this semantic information, the T2I model subsequently refines the transformed samples, helping preserve visual details and semantic information during restoration. Extensive experiments spanning multiple backdoor scenarios, i.e., classification models, CLIP-style encoders, and generative models, demonstrate that SemPurify reliably removes backdoors while effectively preserving semantic information for downstream tasks.

title: MLLM Frame Subset Ensembling for Audio-Visual Video QA and MLLM-based Reranking for Ad-hoc Video Search in TRECVID 2025
authors: Andreas Goulas; Damianos Galanopoulos; Ioannis Patras; Vasileios Mezaris
abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.

title: Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning with Visual Hierarchy for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
authors: Jiyul Ham; Seongho Yoon; Yonggon Jung; Sangjae Lee; Jun-Geol Baek
abstract: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect anomalies in previously unseen classes using auxiliary images, with applications such as industrial visual inspection and medical imaging. Recent vision-language-model-based approaches improve ZSAD by aligning textual and visual representations, while distributional prompting further models prompt variability for unseen categories. However, existing methods do not explicitly combine normality-referenced distributional modeling with hierarchy-specific prompt specialization, limiting their ability to model anomalous semantics relative to normality while addressing both image-level detection and fine-grained localization. We propose Hierarchical Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning (HiDist), a normality-referenced hierarchical distributional prompt framework for ZSAD. HiDist models each prompt token with a diagonal Gaussian distribution and generates stochastic prompt variations through Monte Carlo sampling. Rather than learning normal and anomalous distributions independently, anomalous prompt distributions are parameterized as deviations from learned normal references, explicitly encoding their dependency. The resulting distributions are specialized into global and local representations for image-level detection and pixel-level localization, respectively, while an adapted global visual representation guides hierarchical alignment. Experiments on seven industrial and medical datasets demonstrate strong cross-dataset performance across anomaly detection and localization tasks. Extensive ablation and representation analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed distributional modeling and hierarchy-specific representation learning.

title: Semantic-Critical Regions for Video-to-Audio Generation
authors: Yun Fang; Wei Guo; Zhuonan Liang; Heng Wang; Weidong Cai
abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.

title: Clinically Informed Acoustic-Aware Attribute Modeling for Respiratory Sound Classification
authors: Xinhong Li; Li Xiao; Ziyang Chen; Yuhong Yang; Weiping Tu
abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification (RSC) aims to identify normal and adventitious respiratory sounds, such as crackles and wheezes. Most existing methods formulate RSC as a flat four-class classification problem over norma, crackle, wheeze and both. However, unlike conventional classification tasks with semantically independent and mutually exclusive categories, the commonly used four-class RSC labels have a compositional structure and can be represented by two clinically meaningful sound attributes: crackle presence and wheeze presence. Existing flat classifiers do not explicitly exploit this structure, which may increase the learning burden by treating the four labels as independent targets. Meanwhile, crackles and wheezes exhibit distinct temporal characteristics, with sparse transient crackle events and sustained continuous wheeze patterns, making a single temporal aggregation strategy less suitable for modeling different adventitious sound evidence. To address these limitations, we propose an Acoustic-Aware Asymmetric Framework (AAAF) for RSC. AAAF reformulates four-class recognition as two sound-attribute detection tasks and recovers the final category through logical composition during inference. Built upon a pretrained BEATs encoder, AAAF employs branch-specific multi-layer fusion and asymmetric temporal aggregation to capture localized crackle evidence and sustained wheeze patterns. Auxiliary normal--abnormal supervision and a batch-adaptive dynamic loss are further introduced to improve global discrimination and robustness under imbalanced labels. Experiments on ICBHI and SPRSound demonstrate that AAAF improves overall RSC performance and generalizes across datasets, achieving a state-of-the-art four-class Score of 65.30% on ICBHI.

title: GRAD: Graph-Structured Antibody Defense for LLM Agents
authors: Tianqi Song; Jiawei Du; Xuemei Jia; Zheng Wang
abstract: Memory poisoning and decomposition attacks distribute malicious evidence across the operations of large language model agents. Existing request-level defenses can miss such attacks because they assess individual inputs without connecting earlier information to later actions. Moreover, detectors must adapt as task contexts change, while updates to shared parameters can impair previously learned detection capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose GRAD, which combines graph-based evidence aggregation across operations with an extensible collection of detection experts. Its Semantic-Structural Understanding Module (SSUM) jointly encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed candidate relations in an execution graph to aggregate distributed attack evidence into a graph-level risk score. Its Continual Antibody Adaptation (CAA) adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures, acquiring and reusing detection capabilities as tasks arrive. Across Decomp, MCP, and MRT, GRAD achieves AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60%, respectively, outperforming Sequential Monitor and locally adapted Agent-Sentry and NeuroTaint. CAA improves final accuracy by 13.08 percentage points over Replay on the cross-dataset task stream. The gain remains 9.05 points with equal family/base-case weights within each task. Its compact drop-in gate performs local model inference in milliseconds without monitoring API calls.

title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
authors: Giovanni Vaccarino; Emanuele La Malfa; Dehai Min; Hanrong Zhang; Pier Luca Lanzi; Lu Cheng; Michael J. Wooldridge; Philip S. Yu; Sara Bernardini
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.

title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
authors: Adib Sakhawat; Syed Rifat Raiyan
abstract: Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model-by-language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.

title: Towards Early and Accurate Disease Detection Through Multimodal Predictive Modeling: Fusion of Electronic Health Records, Medical Imaging, And Omics Data Using Interpretable Machine Learning.
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Hayat; Jahangir Baig; Shayan Ahmed; Ahmed Faraz Ayubi
abstract: Early detection of disease is a cornerstone for improving patient outcomes, reducing costs, and enabling preventative interventions. Traditional predictive models often rely on a single type of data (e.g., imaging, clinical labs, or genomics). However, human health is inherently multimodal, involving a variety of data sources such as electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging, wearable sensor data, genomics, and clinical notes. Integrating these heterogeneous modalities into unified predictive modelsoffers a path to richer, more accurate, and more robust disease detection. In this paper, we present a comprehensive survey of methods in multimodal predictive modeling for early disease detection, illustrate architectural patterns and fusion strategies, discuss challenges (e.g. missing modalities, interpretability, generalizability, bias), and highlight promising directions. We also propose a reference architecture for developing such systems and suggest evaluation best practices.

title: Agentic code modernization
authors: Peter F. Peterson; Addi Malviya Thakur
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Software rots. Between refactors for new features, bug fixes, the continual march of cybersecurity advisories, and the slow drift of dependencies toward end-of-life, code must change or cease to exist. The simple act of keeping up can be overwhelming for research software engineers tasked with maintaining long-lived scientific codebases. To address this maintenance burden, the community has developed a vibrant ecosystem of language- and framework-specific tools, such as Dependabot for dependency bumps [1], Clang-Tidy for C++ static analysis [2], and Python Refurb for idiom modernization [3], alongside a host of similar utilities. These tools, while monumental in their contribution, are necessarily limited in scope: they encode a fixed catalog of transformations, they tend to operate on a single file or a single dependency at a time, and they presumably cannot reason about the broader architectural or semantic consequences of a change. More recently, agentic AI systems have arrived. Unlike single-shot code completion, agentic systems can read across a repository, run tests, observe failures, and iterate, and these behaviors, in principle, may enable a different class of modernization task. In this talk, we present concrete examples of modernizing Mantid [4], a more than 20-year-old C++ and Python project with roughly two million lines of code. We attempted to leverage agentic AI to perform maintenance work and modernization work on research software. Changes proposed by the agents were validated against the project's existing automated test suite and reviewed by human maintainers before merging. By exploring successes and failures, the presentation will improve attendees' understanding of when, and with what guardrails, to use AI to assist in modernizing their code. References Dependabot. title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
authors: Yucheng Ruan; Xiang Lan; Jingying Ma; Yizhi Dong; Kai He; Mengling Feng
abstract: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectures, and training objectives; (4) the evolution from adapting traditional Pre-training/Pre-trained language models to the utilization of large language models; (5) an identification of persistent challenges and potential future research directions in language modeling for tabular data analysis. GitHub page associated with this survey is available at: https://github.com/lanxiang1017/Language-Modeling-on-Tabular-Data-Survey.git .

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
authors: Neel Dey; Adrian V. Dalca
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. Our 3D foundation model, anatomix, is used to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes, and we further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system won first place in the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at http://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
authors: Yang Luo; Tiantian Ji; Zifeng Kang; Yucheng Wang; Yong Liu; Zhiyi Yin; Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).

title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
authors: Zongsheng Li; Shengyuan Zhu; Zimo Zhang; Hanyao Li; Shengming Wang; Quanying Liu
abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.

title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
authors: Junming Liu; Marcel Böhme
abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.

title: Harnessing SPAD Noise: Test-Time Gated Attention for Indoor Depth Estimation
authors: Yiquan Gao
abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to hardware-dependent 3D sensing modalities, yet predicting precise metric depth remains a persistent challenge due to intrinsic scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and limited zero-shot generalization in unseen environments. Recent multi-modal approaches incorporate 1D/3D Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) data to resolve these ambiguities, but they mainly treat SPAD noise as a harmful artifact required for denoising or leave the noise ignored. In this paper, we present an essentially different insight: native SPAD noise is an informative prior that implicitly encodes deterministic environmental characteristics. Driven by this paradigm shift, we introduce a novel, lightweight Test-Time Gated Attention framework by Harnessing SPAD Noise, therefore dubbed HSN. Tailored for indoor scenarios, HSN leverages the synergistic combination of 1D SPAD histograms and Gate Adapters (GAs). Through three complementary optimization phases, it generates channel-wise gated attention vectors to dynamically adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, effectively resolving ambiguous scale and boundary challenges without the heavy computational overhead or dense 3D modalities that other TTA methods suffer from. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks show that HSN achieves state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in in-domain settings, while exhibiting even greater potential under zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, interpretability analysis reveals that the proposed gated attention mechanism adaptively shifts attention toward deeper semantic layers under intensifying SPAD noise. Code will be made publicly available.

title: MiDashengLM-Spatial: Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness
authors: Jinbo Hu; Hang Su; Lichun Fan; Heinrich Dinkel; Gang Li; Zhanchen Dai; Yiru Zhang; Chang Liu; Peng Wang; Junnan Wu; Jian Luan; Cong Zou; Heng Qu
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance in general audio understanding, yet most are designed for monaural input and discard the inter-channel cues essential for spatial perception. In contrast, existing spatial audio-language models are purpose-built for spatial tasks and fail to capitalize on the general understanding capabilities of monaural LALMs. We present MiDashengLM-Spatial, the first open-source end-to-end unified audio-language model, to our knowledge, which supports both general audio understanding and spatial awareness within a single architecture. It extends MiDashengLM with a spatial audio encoder, Spatial-Dasheng, integrated through a hierarchical semantic-to-spatial conditioning module that injects intermediate semantic representations into the spatial branch at multiple depths while preserving the original semantic pathway. To provide spatial audio-language supervision at scale, we develop a data synthesis pipeline that renders diverse spatial acoustic scenes with scene-level spatial descriptions and question-answer pairs. Experiments show that Spatial-Dasheng achieves strong performance on sound event localization and detection in real-world scenes, and that MiDashengLM-Spatial substantially outperforms existing LALMs on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Meanwhile, it remains competitive with state-of-the-art 8B-scale LALMs on diverse monaural benchmarks, demonstrating that spatial awareness can be acquired without compromising general audio understanding. The source code and model checkpoint are available at https://github.com/xiaomi-research/midashenglm-spatial and https://huggingface.co/mispeech/midashenglm-spatial.

title: TwinViT-DeepJSCC: Adversarially Robust Semantic Image Communication
authors: Maedeh Fallahreyhani; Paeiz Azmi; Nader Mokari; M. Reza Abedi; Melike Erol-Kantarci; Eduard A. Jorswieck
abstract: Learning-based semantic communication is vulnerable to adversarial perturbations introduced before semantic encoding or over wireless channels. This paper proposes TwinViT-DeepJSCC, a preventive-corrective semantic image transceiver operating under a fixed channel-use budget. Two Vision Transformer (ViT)-based deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) branches learn complementary latent representations protected by sensitivity-aware masking. At the receiver, confidence-aware fusion, blind corruption-severity estimation, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)-severity-conditioned denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) purification mitigate residual corruption without requiring attack metadata. Experiments on the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research 100-class (CIFAR-100) dataset consider fast gradient sign method (FGSM), projected gradient descent (PGD), natural evolution strategies (NES), and Carlini-Wagner (CW) source-domain attacks, as well as random jamming and channel-aware adversarial waveforms over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and block-flat Rayleigh fading. Under matched channel-use and attack budgets, TwinViT-DeepJSCC achieves maximum peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of approximately 9.5 dB under 20-step PGD and 10.8 dB under channel-aware waveform attacks over block-flat Rayleigh fading. Under PGD, it also improves Top-1 accuracy by up to approximately 38 percentage points over the undefended baseline and 13 percentage points over the strongest competing defense. Ablation results confirm the complementary contributions of the proposed transmitter- and receiver-side mechanisms.

title: Visual-Invariance-Augmented Feature Optimal Alignment for Transferable Adversarial Attacks against Closed-Source MLLMs
authors: Xiaojun Jia; Simeng Qin; Yiming Li; Jie Liao; Sensen Gao; Ke Ma; Yang Liu; Xiaochun Cao
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain vulnerable to transferable adversarial examples, especially in black-box settings where only open-source surrogate models are accessible. Existing targeted transfer attacks mainly align adversarial and target samples using global image-level features, such as encoder [CLS] embeddings. However, such coarse alignment insufficiently exploits patch-level visual structures, limiting transferability across heterogeneous closed-source MLLMs. We propose IAU-FOA, a visual-invariance-augmented feature optimal alignment attack with adaptive unbalanced transport, to improve targeted transferability against closed-source MLLMs. IAU-FOA aligns adversarial and target samples at both global and local levels: a cosine-based objective narrows their global semantic gap, while patch tokens are clustered into compact local patterns and matched through optimal transport for fine-grained feature alignment. Balanced optimal transport enforces fixed marginal masses even for local clusters without reliable counterparts, potentially introducing misleading alignment gradients. We therefore introduce confidence-adaptive unbalanced transport to relax these constraints for weakly matched clusters, aiming to reduce unreliable local alignment and improve adversarial transferability. We further study the effect of input transformations and propose visual-invariance augmentation, which applies bidirectional pixel-intensity rescaling and per-channel white-balance adjustment to simulate exposure, contrast, illumination, and color-temperature variations. This strategy encourages adversarial perturbations to generalize across different visual encoders. Extensive experiments on open-source and closed-source MLLMs show that IAU-FOA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transferable attack methods. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaxiaojunQAQ/IAU-FOA.

title: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset
authors: Mohammad Abolnejadian; Matthew Brehmer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Canadian Parliament Open Data and Embedded Vector Knowledge Base: InsightToast (UIST '26) Supplemental Dataset 📄 Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3830398.3830522💻 Code: https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast Supplemental dataset for the paper: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings Mohammad Abolnejadian and Matthew Brehmer. Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '26). DOI: 10.1145/3830398.3830522 This dataset provides a collection of 43,878 open legislative records from the Canadian House of Commons, spanning 1994 to 2025, covering document types such as debates (Hansard), legislative bills, committee reports, petitions, recorded votes, order papers, and Library of Parliament research publications. It is released at three stages of the same pipeline: the raw collected documents, a processed corpus that has been passed through an ETL pipeline and chunked for use in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, and an embedded, pre-indexed vector store built from that processed corpus. The dataset supports the development and user study of the InsightToast project. The embedded form can be placed directly into the project's codebase, open sourced at https://github.com/ubixgroup/InsightToast, where it serves as the knowledge base when InsightToast operates as a proactive side-channel assistant in policy discussion meetings. Usage in the InsightToast Backend Only qdrant_storage.tar.gz is required to run the backend. Extract it into the root of the InsightToast project, so that qdrant_storage/ sits alongside docker-compose.yml, and start the services: tar -xzf qdrant_storage.tar.gz -C /path/to/InsightToast/ cd /path/to/InsightToast docker compose up --build -d Contents File What it is Approx. size parliament_data.tar.gz Raw source corpus of 43,878 parliamentary records, as 57,124 files (.txt + .pdf) 8.1 GB compressed / 11 GB extracted parliament_data_processed.tar.gz Processed corpus: the same records cleaned, normalized, and chunked into RAG-ready JSON 2.1 GB compressed / 9.1 GB extracted qdrant_storage.tar.gz Pre-indexed Qdrant vector store, ready to mount as the knowledge base 21 GB compressed / 27 GB extracted parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the raw corpus, viewable without downloading the archive small parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the processed corpus small qdrant_storage.STRUCTURE.txt Manifest of the vector store small SHA256SUMS.txt SHA-256 checksums for the three archives small Verify the archives after download: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt Source Corpus: Raw Parliamentary Documents parliament_data.tar.gz contains open legislative documents collected across the range of record types produced by the Canadian House of Commons and the Library of Parliament, including the proceedings of debate, the texts of bills as tabled, the reports of standing committees, the petitions presented to the House, and the recorded outcomes of divisions. The documents were assembled from three public sources: the House of Commons (ourcommons.ca, including the Legislative Information service, LEGISinfo), the Library of Parliament of Canada (parl-gc.primo.exlibrisgroup.com), and the independent open-data mirror openparliament.ca. No private, personal, or access-restricted material is included; Member of Parliament profiles contain only information published in an official public capacity. Total: 43,878 parliamentary records, distributed across 57,124 files (43,634 .txt + 13,490 .pdf). Each record is provided as extracted plain text, with the source PDF alongside it under the same basename where one exists, so records that carry both formats account for two files. Temporal coverage: documents span the 35th through 45th Parliaments. Debates run from 1994-01-17 to 2025-10-10; coverage of the other record types varies by type. Languages: the source records are bilingual (English and French), as published by Parliament. Filename conventions: debates use sitting dates (YYYY-MM-DD- .txt); bills, journals, order papers, and votes use - - (for example, 37-1-C-10); petitions and Library of Parliament publications use slugified titles. Category Files Description debates/ 18,347 House of Commons debates (Hansard transcripts), one file per sitting day bills/ 10,561 Legislative bills, full text plus the original tabled PDF journals/ 7,038 Official Journals of the House (daily record of decisions) petitions/ 6,093 e-Petitions and paper petitions presented to the House votes/ 4,521 Recorded division and vote results order-papers/ 4,228 Order Paper and Notice Paper (daily agenda) library/ 2,202 Library of Parliament publications and tabled agreements committee-reports/ 1,577 Standing and joint committee reports, grouped into 27 committee subfolders politicians/ 1,319 Member of Parliament profiles research/ 1,210 Library of Parliament research and HillNotes publications committees/ 28 Committee mandate and description summaries Total 57,124 See parliament_data.STRUCTURE.txt for the full breakdown, including all committee subfolders. Processed Corpus: Cleaned and Chunked Records parliament_data_processed.tar.gz contains the same corpus after the ETL pipeline that turns each document into retrievable units. Documents are parsed from their metadata header and routed by document_type. Bilingual records are language-identified with langdetect and reduced to their English content by an LLM pass. PDFs are structurally partitioned with unstructured's partition_pdf into text, table, and image elements; table elements are linearized into prose by an LLM, and salient figures are captioned, written to images/, and linked from their chunk via has_images. Records whose content is inherently tabular, namely recorded votes, petitions, and Member profiles, are rendered into natural-language narratives to keep them semantically retrievable rather than reducing to fields. Type-specific pre-segmentation then splits debates on speaker turns, preserving the speaker, section, and timestamp, before every stream passes through a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (1,000 characters, 200 overlap); each resulting chunk is tagged with its content_type (text, table, or image) and its provenance. The output is one JSON document per record, holding the record's metadata and its ordered list of chunks: { "metadata": { "document_type": "debate", "session": "35-1", "date": "1994-01-17", "language": "en", "source_file": "debates/1994-01-17-1.txt", "source_url": "...", "total_chunks": 51 }, "chunks": [ { "chunk_id": 0, "content": "...", "metadata": { "speaker": "...", "section": "...", "content_type": "text", "has_images": false } } ] } Volume: 42,014 JSON records and 2,170 extracted images, totaling 6,379,732 chunks, which is the set embedded into the knowledge base below. Traceability: every record's metadata.source_file links back to its file in the raw corpus. Coverage: most record types are processed in full; committee-report and library are present as subsets of the raw corpus. See parliament_data_processed.STRUCTURE.txt for per-category counts. Indexed Knowledge Base qdrant_storage.tar.gz contains the processed corpus above embedded and indexed into Qdrant, ready to serve as the retrieval backend with no further processing. Collection Size Vectors Role parliament_documents ~27 GB 768-dim, cosine Primary knowledge base retrieved during meetings vega_altair_docs ~137 MB 768-dim, cosine Vega-Altair documentation used by the visualization-generator agent Embedding model: embeddinggemma:latest (served via Ollama), 768 dimensions, cosine distance. Qdrant version: built with qdrant/qdrant:v1.13.6. Qdrant's on-disk format is version-specific, so load this snapshot with the same or a compatible version to avoid migration issues. title: Provable Coordination for LLM Agents via Message Sequence Charts
authors: Benedikt Bollig; Matthias Függer; Thomas Nowak
abstract: Abstract Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are difficult to reason about. Coordination errors such as deadlocks or type-mismatched messages are often hard to detect through testing. We introduce a domain-specific language for specifying agent coordination based on message sequence charts (MSCs). The language separates message-passing structure from LLM calls, tool calls, and human control points, whose outcomes remain unpredictable. We define the syntax and semantics of the language and present a syntax-directed projection that generates deadlock-free local agent programs from global coordination specifications. We illustrate the approach with a diagnosis consensus protocol and show how coordination properties can be established independently of LLM nondeterminism. We also describe a runtime planning extension in which an LLM dynamically generates a coordination workflow for which the same structural guarantees apply. An open-source Python implementation of our framework is available as ZipperGen.
